title: Fewest Tokens Making An Exact Amount
statement: You are given up to 12 distinct token values, each a positive integer up to two million, and a target amount up to 10,000. An unlimited supply of each token value is available. Report the fewest tokens whose values add up to exactly the target, or negative one when no combination reaches it exactly. A target of zero needs no tokens at all.

canonicalLadder.frame: Input: up to 12 distinct token values and a target up to 10,000, with unlimited supply of each value. Output: the fewest tokens, or negative one. Note which magnitude bounds the state space — it is the target, not the number of token values.
canonicalLadder.brute: Recurse on the remaining amount: try each token value that fits, subtract it, and recurse; take the best result plus one. The branching factor is the number of token values and the depth is the target divided by the smallest value, so the tree is exponential.
canonicalLadder.bottleneck: The fewest tokens needed for a given remaining amount depends only on that amount, yet the recursion recomputes it once for every distinct order and combination of earlier tokens that leaves that amount — reaching an amount of 4,000 by hundreds of thousands of different routes triggers hundreds of thousands of identical computations.
canonicalLadder.lift: Cache on the remaining amount alone. There are only 10,001 possible remaining amounts, so memoizing bounds the work at the target times the number of token values, about 120,000 constant-time steps.
canonicalLadder.invariant: The stored value for an amount is always the fewest tokens summing to exactly that amount, or a marker for unreachable; it is computed from amounts strictly smaller, so a sweep upward from zero always reads finished entries.
canonicalLadder.verify: A target of zero, giving zero; a target smaller than every token value, giving negative one; a single token value that divides the target and one that does not; a token value equal to the target; a case where taking the largest value first is wrong, such as values of 1, 3 and 4 with a target of 6; the maximum target with the maximum number of values. Time proportional to the target times the value count, space proportional to the target.

hints: Two magnitudes are given and only one of them bounds the search space. Twelve token values, a target of 10,000 — say which one determines how many distinct situations the solver can ever be in.
You have a recursion that subtracts a token value and recurses on what is left. Say what the recursion needs to know at any call in order to finish.

It needs only the remaining amount. Every different order and combination of earlier tokens that leaves the same remaining amount faces identical remaining work, and your recursion redoes that work for each of them.
Name the waste: recomputing the fewest tokens for a remaining amount that has already been solved, where the amount alone determines the answer and the route to it is irrelevant.
Store the answer for each remaining amount the first time it is computed. Memoizing the brute force bounds the total work at the number of distinct amounts times the number of token values.

Fill an array indexed by amount, from zero upward. The entry at zero is zero; the entry at an amount is one plus the smallest entry at that amount minus each token value that fits and is itself reachable, or the unreachable marker if none is. Answer at the target. Why must the sweep run upward from zero, and what makes each entry final the moment it is written?

Frame: up to 12 distinct token values up to two million each, a target up to 10,000, unlimited supply; output is the fewest tokens or negative one. The target, not the value count, bounds the state space — a large token value simply never fits and is irrelevant. Brute: recurse on the remaining amount, trying each value that fits; branching factor up to 12 and depth up to the target divided by the smallest value, so exponential. Bottleneck: the answer for a remaining amount depends only on that amount, yet it is recomputed once for every combination and ordering of earlier tokens leaving that amount, which is hundreds of thousands of identical computations for a mid-range amount. Lift: memoize on the amount. With only 10,001 distinct amounts, the work is bounded by target times value count, about 120,000 constant-time steps. Invariant: the entry for an amount is the fewest tokens summing exactly to it, or an unreachable marker. Each entry depends only on strictly smaller amounts, which is what makes an upward sweep valid and each entry final when written. Verify: a target of zero gives zero, a target below every value gives negative one, a value dividing the target gives the quotient, a value equal to the target gives one, and values of 1, 3 and 4 with a target of 6 give two rather than the three that taking the largest value first would produce — that case is the standard refutation of the obvious local rule. Time O(target times value count), space O(target). Unlimited supply is what makes the sweep ascending; the bounded-supply variant requires a descending sweep instead, and the two are worth contrasting.

distractors.temptingBecause: Repeatedly taking the largest token that fits is how people actually make change and it is correct for ordinary currency systems, which makes it feel proven. It has no exchange argument for arbitrary value sets — 1, 3 and 4 with a target of 6 defeats it immediately.

Every token costs one, so this is genuinely a shortest path over amounts and a layered sweep gives the right answer. It is the same computation with a queue instead of an array, and it obscures the recurrence the problem exists to derive.

Enumerating token combinations with pruning is the honest brute force and the derivation legitimately starts there. It stops being the answer the moment you notice that only the remaining amount matters, not which tokens produced it.

misleadingFingerprint: Twelve token values is a small-n signal that suggests enumeration or bitmask methods, and the making-change framing is one people have a working real-world heuristic for; the target, which is the real state dimension, is stated almost in passing.
edgeCases: a target smaller than every token value
a token value equal to the target
a single token value dividing the target
a single token value not dividing the target
values of 1, 3 and 4 with a target of 6
the maximum target with the maximum number of values

drillVariants.statement: Given up to 12 distinct positive token values with unlimited supply of each and a target amount up to 10,000, report the fewest tokens summing to exactly the target, or negative one if none can. Enumerating combinations is exponential. Name the mechanism and the repeated operation it eliminates.

A vending machine dispenses change using up to 12 denominations of an unusual currency, with an unlimited stock of each. Given an amount up to 10,000 units to return, it must use as few physical pieces as possible, or refuse if the amount cannot be made exactly. The obvious rule of always dispensing the largest piece that fits is known to fail for this currency. Enumerating combinations is hopeless. What mechanism applies, and what wasted work does it remove?
